35 A cell of constant electromotive force drives a current I through an external resistor of
resistance R. The terminal potential difference (p.d.) across the cell is V.

When the internal resistance r of the cell increases, what is the effect on V and on I?

hints: Notice the e.m.f. $E$ and external resistance $R$ are fixed while only internal resistance $r$ increases, so total resistance $R+r$ increases.
Recall $I = E/(R+r)$ for the loop and $V = IR$ across the external resistor, which is also $V = E - Ir$.
Compare the new smaller $I$ with $V = IR$: with $R$ constant, decide whether $V$ must rise or fall when $I$ falls.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit: e.m.f. $E$ is constant, external resistor $R$ is constant, internal resistance $r$ increases. Total resistance in the single loop is $R+r$.
State the current rule: $E = I(R+r)$, so $I = E/(R+r)$. With numerator $E$ fixed and denominator larger, $I$ decreases.
State the terminal p.d. rule: $V$ is the p.d. across $R$, so $V = IR$. It is also the e.m.f. minus lost volts, $V = E - Ir$.
Apply the change: $R$ is unchanged and $I$ is smaller, so the product $IR$ is smaller and $V$ decreases.
This combined decrease in $I$ and decrease in $V$ matches the row with decreases and decreases. This is option A.

A.explanation: Total resistance $R+r$ increases so $I$ falls, and $V = IR$ with fixed $R$ therefore also falls.

B.explanation: Current cannot increase when total resistance $R+r$ increases with constant e.m.f.

C.explanation: Terminal p.d. $V = IR$ must fall when $I$ falls because external $R$ is unchanged.

D.explanation: Both $I$ and $V$ cannot increase when a larger $r$ opposes the same e.m.f.
